# Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving

The backend and frontend changes now exist in two repositories.  A passing test in either
repository may not, by itself, show that the change is complete.  This chapter separates the
evidence gathered by validation, implementation review, synchronization, and archival.

## Learning objective

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to validate the OpenSpec artifacts, compare the
implementation with the accepted change, synchronize accepted deltas into the main specifications,
and archive a completed change without losing its history.

## Four different checks

These checks address different questions.  Running one generally does not replace the others.

| Check | Question it answers | Evidence it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact validation | Are the proposal, requirements, design, and tasks structured correctly? | The OpenSpec CLI result and any reported structural errors |
| Implementation verification | Does the code and its test suite implement the accepted behavior? | Code review, focused tests, integration evidence, and the task status |
| Synchronization | Have accepted requirements moved into the main specifications? | Updated main specs and the retained change record |
| Archival | Is the change complete and recoverable after active work closes? | An archived change containing its reason, decisions, and evidence |

Artifact validation is usually the cheapest check, so you might run it first.  It can catch a malformed artifact or a
missing required section.  It cannot prove that the application behaves correctly, that the tests
exercise the right path, or that the two repositories agree.

## Validate the artifacts

Run the OpenSpec validation command configured for the repository.  You will usually want to validate the backend and frontend change
directories separately because each repository owns its own code, tests,
and specification context.

Read the result rather than treating a successful exit code as the whole review.  Check
that the validator examined the expected change and that the reported paths match the artifacts you
edited.
If validation fails, repair the artifact structure before asking Copilot to inspect the
implementation.  A code review built on an incomplete change description may otherwise have no
stable target.

Validation also has a useful limit: it checks the shape and rules the CLI knows about.  It does not
decide whether a requirement is complete, whether a design is coherent, or whether an accepted
scenario works in a running application.

## Verify the implementation

Compare the implementation with the proposal, requirements, design, and tasks.  It helps to start
with the requirements and scenarios because they describe the behavior a user or another system can
observe.  You can then use the design and tasks to check whether the implementation follows the
agreed boundaries.

For the unit-number change, one useful inspection order follows the contract:

1. Verify the backend behavior and its API document.
2. Check that the frontend client was generated from that reviewed API document.
3. Check the frontend states against the frontend requirements.
4. Run the cross-repository path and confirm the browser-visible result.

This order can make a contract mismatch easier to locate.  If the backend behavior or API document
is wrong, the backend-owned artifact is the natural place to repair it.  If the contract is correct but the UI is
missing a scenario, the frontend implementation or its tests may need the repair.  Adding an undocumented workaround to one repository
can make the other appear complete without resolving the underlying gap.

Use the task list as a checklist, not as proof.  A completed task means that someone marked it
complete.  The tests and review still need to show that the accepted behavior works and that the
implementation remains coherent with the design.

## Synchronize accepted changes

Synchronization moves an accepted delta into the main specifications.  In OpenSpec 1.13.1, it is
useful to treat `sync` as a specification update, not as a code-generation or test command.  Before
running it, check that the implementation is complete, the tests pass, and the change has been accepted
by the team.

Inspect the main specifications before synchronization.  Note which requirements already exist,
which are new, and which accepted behavior the delta changes.  Then run the repository's configured
`sync` workflow and inspect the resulting diff.  Look for the accepted behavior in the
main specifications, while checking that conditions remain present and the change record remains intact.

Repeat the inspection after synchronization.  Check that:

- the main specifications describe the behavior now implemented;
- unchanged requirements remain unchanged;
- the delta still records why the change was made; and
- identifiers such as the Jira issue and cross-repository change identifier remain attached.

If the diff changes more than the accepted delta, pause and review the generated or proposed update.
Treat synchronization as a specification update, rather than a way to resolve ambiguity by editing
the specification until it fits the code.

## Archive only completed work

Archiving closes the active change after its accepted behavior has been synchronized and verified.
Ideally, it leaves a future reader enough context to understand what changed, why it changed,
and where the supporting evidence came from.

Before archiving the backend and frontend changes, confirm that:

- artifact validation succeeds in both repositories;
- implementation tasks are complete;
- focused tests and the cross-repository path pass;
- main specifications are coherent after synchronization; and
- the change record preserves its Jira and cross-repository identifiers.

Archive the changes using the repository's configured OpenSpec workflow.  Inspect the archive after
the operation.  A moved directory would not be sufficient if the archive had lost the proposal,
requirements, design, tasks, or the reason for the change.

You will generally want to archive the two repositories only when their completion states agree.  If the
backend is ready but the frontend still has an open scenario, consider keeping the active work
open and recording the missing evidence.  The archive is most useful when it describes completed
work rather than a hopeful stopping point.

## The fresh-session test

A useful check after archival is to start a new Copilot session.  Provide the repository artifacts,
not the previous chat transcript, and ask what the unit-number change requires.  See whether the session can recover the
accepted behavior from the main specifications and the archived change.

This test can expose decisions that still exist only in someone's memory.  When the fresh session
cannot recover a condition, identifier, or boundary, return to the specifications or archive and
record it there.  A remembered conversation does not belong to the repository's
source of truth.

## Hands-on exercise

Validate, verify, synchronize when appropriate, and archive the unit-number changes in both
repositories.

1. Run artifact validation in each repository and repair any structural failure.
2. Compare the backend and frontend implementation with their accepted requirements, designs, and
	tasks.
3. Run the focused tests and the cross-repository verification path.
4. Inspect the main specifications, synchronize the accepted deltas, and review the resulting diff.
5. Preserve the Jira and cross-repository identifiers, then archive only after both repositories
	meet the completion conditions.
6. Start a fresh Copilot session and recover the accepted behavior from repository artifacts.

## Verification checkpoint

The unit-number change may be ready to close when the main specifications are coherent, active
tasks are complete, the tests and cross-repository path pass, and the archived artifacts preserve
the reason for the change.  If any of those conditions is missing, consider leaving the change active
and recording the missing evidence.

## What you learned

Validation checks artifact structure.  Tests and review verify behavior.  Synchronization records
accepted behavior in the main specifications.  Archiving closes the active change while preserving
the decisions and identifiers needed to recover it later.
